catalog_quote: 10.2 Stress algorithm. The word-stress algorithm, as put forward in the available literature on Maaloula Aramaic (e.g., Bergsträsser 1915: xxi; Spitaler 1938: 46; Arnold 1990a: 40), is given in (1). ... (1) Maaloula Aramaic stress algorithm (according to the available literature) (a) Stress the final syllable if it has a long vowel or ends with two consonants or a geminate: mal.kṓ ‘kings’ ... ray.šáyn ‘their heads’ ... riḥ.máčč ‘she loved me’ (b) Otherwise stress the penultimate syllable: ṯár.ʕa ‘door’ ... ḥaẓ.ẓū́.ra ‘apple’ ... ṯi.na.ġél.ča ‘hen’ ... (4) Maaloula Aramaic stress algorithm (revised moraic version) (a) Stress the final syllable if it is bimoraic: ... (b) Otherwise stress the penultimate syllable if it is bimoraic: ... (c) Otherwise stress the penultimate syllable in disyllabic words and stress the antepenultimate syllable in polysyllabic words: ... This algorithm shows that Maaloula Aramaic has a three-syllable window at the right word edge, which means that stress must fall on the final, penultimate, or antepenultimate syllable of the word. Maaloula Aramaic shows a strong tendency to place stress on one of the last two syllables. It is only when the final and penultimate syllables are light (i.e., monomoraic) in polysyllabic words that stress can be placed on the antepenultimate syllable, regardless of its weight.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable from syllable weight within a three-syllable window at the right edge: a bimoraic final syllable (long vowel, or closed by two consonants or a geminate) takes stress; otherwise a bimoraic penult takes stress; if both final and penult are light, stress falls on the penult in disyllables and on the antepenult in longer words. The default (and by far most frequent) outcome is penultimate stress, with final stress on heavy finals. Jastrow 1997: 336 and Bergsträsser 1915: XXI state the same final-if-heavy-else-penult rule; Eid's corpus study adds the light-light antepenult case. Only one long vowel per word, always in the stressed syllable; unstressed (pretonic) vowels shorten and mid vowels raise.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Eid 2024 does not discuss secondary stress. Bergsträsser 1915: XX-XXI mentions a 'Gegenton' (counter-accent, marked with the same acute) in longer complexes but gives no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Arnold 1990: 40-41, 328 notes CVCVCa loanwords with antepenult stress (sálaṭa 'salad', mákana 'car', sínama 'cinema'); Eid 2024: 215 finds ~70 antepenult-stressed word forms, not all loans, all with light penult and light final, and folds them into rule (4c). Bergsträsser 1915: XX notes sentence-level shifts (verb stressed on its final syllable before an immediately following object; proclitic/enclitic words lose stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; corpus word forms from the Maaloula Aramaic Speech Corpus (published texts of Arnold 1991a/b, Bergsträsser 1915 etc.). Phrase-level shifts and de-stressing of clitics described by Bergsträsser 1915: XX-XXI. All three statements are for the Ma'lula dialect; Jastrow 1997 frames the rule for WNA generally with Ma'lula examples.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand statements describe the Ma'lula (Maaloula) dialect of Western Neo-Aramaic [west2763 / amw]; Eid 2024 is explicitly Ma'lula-only (corpus of Ma'lula texts), Jastrow 1997 frames the rule for WNA as a whole with Ma'lula examples, Bergsträsser 1915 is Ma'lula. Bakh'a and Jubb'adin are covered only in Arnold 1990 (not opened). Glottolog attaches Maclean 1895 (NENA) and Jacobi 1973 (Turoyo) to this languoid in error; both are ignored here.

new_statements.quote: p. 68 (PDF p. 72): "Die Druckeinheit, für gewöhnlich identisch mit der „Gruppe“, besitzt in der Regel einen Druckgipfel, seltener einen Haupt- und einen Nebengipfel; der Gipfel fällt auf eine den Wortdruck tragende Silbe, nur selten auf eine im isolierten Einzelwert drucklose (Druckverschiebung)." p. 97 fn. 1 (PDF p. 101): "Ein verhältnismäßig seltener Fall, da der Dialekt Länge nach dem Wortdruck nicht kennt, also für einen solchen Schluß nur einsilbige oder endbetonte Worte in Frage kommen, und solche sind nicht häufig." p. 4 (PDF p. 8), Zeichenerklärung: "Kurzer Bindestrich - bezeichnet nach Verbalform vor der Präposition l enge Bindung und Endbetontheit der Verbalform."
new_statements.translation: p. 68: 'The stress unit, usually identical with the "group", as a rule has one stress peak, more rarely a main and a secondary peak; the peak falls on a syllable that carries the word stress, only rarely on one that is unstressed in the isolated single word (stress shift).' p. 97 fn. 1: 'A relatively rare case, since the dialect does not have [vowel] length after the word stress, so that for such a [group] ending only monosyllabic or end-stressed words come into question, and such are not frequent.' p. 4: 'A short hyphen - after a verbal form before the preposition l marks close binding and end-stress of the verbal form.'

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Eid 2024: final syllable stressed if it has a long vowel / CC / geminate, else penult; weight-sensitive): Bergsträsser 1933 takes that word-stress placement as given (his own 1915 statement is one of Eid's cited sources) and adds phrase-level detail -- no post-tonic vowel length, end-stressed words infrequent, end-stress of verb forms before enclitic l-, and rare sentence-level stress shifts (mostly to the initial syllable) in connected speech. It does not itself formulate the word-stress algorithm, so it neither confirms nor alters the weight criterion; nothing in it contradicts the catalog. the compilers guess (instrumental study of phrase-level prosody…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The monograph is an instrumental/auditory study of SENTENCE stress (Druckverteilung) and sentence melody in phonograph recordings; it presupposes the word-stress position of each word as already known ('Drucklage im Wort', Einleitung p. 3; 'den Wortdruck tragende Silbe', p. 68) and never restates the word-stress rule (for which Eid 2024 cites Bergsträsser 1915: xxi). What it does say about word stress: (i) every stress group has its peak on a syllable that carries word stress; only rarely does the peak land on a syllable that is unstressed in the isolated word (Druckverschiebung, pp. 68, 94-96: mostly initial stress at the start of a falling curve, very rarely a shift toward the word end, e.g. end-stressing of a participle to obtain a rising-falling curve; occasional double stress in long or emphatic words); (ii) the dialect has no vowel length after the word stress, so a long final syllable arises only in monosyllables or end-stressed words, 'and such are not frequent' (p. 97 fn. 1) -- i.e. word stress is normally non-final and final stress is the marked case tied to the word's shape, consistent with the catalogued rule (final if CVV/CVCC, else penult) without stating it; (iii) a verbal form closely bound to a following preposition l- is end-stressed (Zeichenerklärung p. 4; p. 96 'endbetonte Verbalformen mit enklitischem l-'); (iv) stress and pitch run largely parallel: the stressed syllable is also the higher one (pp. 68, 96); weak secondary stress (Nebendruck) occurs at group level and has no noticeable pitch effect (p. 69).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only at the level of the stress group: weaker word-stress syllables of 'second' and 'third' grade rise toward and fall away from the group peak; 'Gelegentlicher Nebendruck (‘) ist schwach und nicht von merklicher Tonwirkung begleitet' (p. 69). Two stresses within one word are noted only for a few long, emphatic or rhythmically alternating words (p. 96: N 373, N 374-376, K 10). Nothing on lexical secondary stress within the word.
new_statements.exceptions: Druckverschiebung (pp. 94-96): in connected speech the group peak occasionally falls on a syllable unstressed in isolation -- most often initial stress at the beginning of a falling curve (listed examples N 165, E 3, N 90, 324/5, 420, 27, 342, 125, B 6, N 103/4, 253, D 4, G 10, N 55), once group-internally (C 8), content-driven stem stress instead of ending stress in a contrast pair (N 238), very rarely a shift toward the word end (N 234a, end-stressing of a participle), and by grammatical analogy some verb forms are treated like end-stressed forms with enclitic l- (N 254, E 4, N 272, N 252, N 226). Verbal form + preposition l-: end-stressed (p. 4).
new_statements.identity_note: The Neo-Aramaic dialect of Ma'lula (Malula), Anti-Lebanon, Syria = Maaloula Aramaic (west2763); recordings made in Damascus in spring 1914 (texts A-L) and spring 1930 (M-O) from the speaker 'Aptalla M'allmona of Ma'lula (c. 16 years old in 1914) and, for K and L, his age-mates Selim 'Isa and Nasif of Malula (Einleitung p. 1).

new_statements.quote: p. 5: "In Maaloula Aramaic, word stress falls on the final CVV(C0) or CVCC syllable.6 Otherwise, it falls on the penultimate syllable (Arnold, 1990: 40; Bergsträsser, 1915: xxi; Spitaler, 1938: 46). The epenthetic schwa seems to be considered non-syllabic because it is not visible to stress (see Bergsträsser, 1915: xix)." [fn. 6: "C0 refers to any number of consonants including zero."] pp. 17-18, (32): "(a) Stress the final syllable if it is bimoraic ... (b) Otherwise stress the penultimate syllable if it is bimoraic ... (c) If neither the final nor the penultimate syllable is bimoraic, stress the penultimate syllable in disyllabic words and stress the antepenultimate syllable in polysyllabic words"

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and same type as the existing statement from Eid 2024 (The Phonology of Maaloula Aramaic, ch. 10, pp. 214/216): final if heavy (CVV(C0)/CVCC), else penult, with the moraic revision adding antepenult when final and penult are both light in polysyllables. The book's ch. 8 is explicitly a later version of this article (book p. 144 n. 1), and (32) here is the same three-clause moraic algorithm as the book's (4). Adds relative to the catalog record (which has an empty rule): explicit weight criteria (final CVC light by extrametricality), lexical ordering of stress before epenthesis, and the reclassification of Arnold's 'exceptions' as regular antepenultimate cases. Confidence high.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive right-edge stress: a final syllable is stressed if heavy (long vowel with any coda, or short vowel + CC; word-final CVC counts as light via final-consonant extrametricality, p. 11 fn. 16); otherwise the penult is stressed if heavy (CVV or closed CVC); if both final and penult are light, stress is penultimate in disyllables and antepenultimate in longer words (e.g. ˈʕarabeṯ 'Arabic', ˈʕaliṯa 'leaf', mičˈrattitin). Stress is assigned lexically, so syllables whose nucleus is the postlexical epenthetic schwa are invisible to stress (ˈno.šəḳ.ṯa 'kiss', not *no.ˈšəḳ.ṯa).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress; p. 12-13 (the text) states each phonological word has one main stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Fn. 18 (p. 17): clause (c) was added 'to accommodate the polysyllabic words treated in the literature as exceptions to the stress rule (see Arnold, 1990: 41). We do not consider them exceptions since they systematically adhere to (c).' Epenthetic-schwa syllables never bear or count for stress (sec. 2.3 p. 5-6, sec. 3.5 p. 17, sec. 4 the text: Maaloula Aramaic has no lexical epenthesis, hence no epenthesis-stress interaction).
new_statements.identity_note: The article describes the Western Neo-Aramaic dialect of Maaloula specifically (p. 1: 'the term Maaloula Aramaic will be used throughout the paper to denote the Western Neo-Aramaic dialect of Maaloula'), not Bakhaa or Jubbaadin; data from Arnold's published texts (vols. III-IV) plus elicitation with one native-speaker consultant (Emad Rihan).
